title: Bouncing ball

reference.basis: cartoon illustration with no guaranteed standard size, so not used as a ruler

slow_motion.evidence: No caption, narration or visual effect indicates slow motion.

subjects.description: small glossy red spherical ball falling and bouncing vertically

observation.what_happens: A small red ball drops vertically from beneath a pinned paper toward a brown floor. It impacts the floor and bounces repeatedly, rising to progressively lower heights.

calibration.note: scale from the fall itself: 340 px/s² over 3 arcs = g of 9.807 m/s²

given: g = 9.807 m/s² (Earth); it set the scale, so treat g as known and fixed
reasoning: y falls parabolically from 0 to about -9 m, then rises to about -3.5 m and falls again, while x drifts steadily, so flight is projectile under g with a floor bounce losing energy. Apex ratio implies e near 0.78. On Earth in air over ~9 m fall drag may show, so we compete no-drag vs linear vs quadratic drag, all with the same restitution bounce.

headline: Ball falls freely and bounces lower each time
finding: The ball falls under gravity 9.81 m/s², hits the floor at -9.03 ± 0.025 m and bounces back keeping 0.78 ± 0.00036 of its speed. Each bounce rises lower than the last with almost no air slowing it.

eyeball.confidence: low, rough pixel ratios from few frames and assumed US Letter paper scale
eyeball.law_in_words: For free fall v^2 = 2 g h, so normal restitution v_after/v_before = sqrt(h_apex_after / h_apex_before); absolute scale from standard paper sheet height ~0.28 m compared to brown board height in image.
